To the Minister for Child Protection and the Chief Executive of the Department for Child Protection, I recommend that (if Recommendation 40 of ‘The Life They Deserve’ is not to be implemented) a policy be developed which identifies the circumstances in which a notifier is to be advised, or not advised, that a notification has been closed with no action. Fisher, Lynne Patricia (Coroner Kereru) I make the following recommendations directed to the Minister for Health and Wellbeing and the Royal Australian College of General Practitioners. 1)   That the Royal Australian College of General Practitioners release an alert to its members educating them on, and explaining the importance of, the risk scores and ‘red flags’ relating to community acquired pneumonia; and 2)   That SA Health release an alert to all South Australian Licensed Private Hospitals that treat patients in an emergency setting educating them on, and explaining the importance of, the risk score and ‘red flags’ relating to community acquired pneumonia. Jablanovic, Branko (Coroner Whittle) I recommend that the Cardiac Society of Australia and New Zealand, in conjunction with the Royal Australian College of General Practitioners, consider whether it is necessary to alert the general practice community to the risks involved in the prescription of propranolol in untreated cardiac failure. Lens, Christopher (Coroner White) I support the recommendation of the investigating officer in this matter and recommend that a complete review of all detention orders be undertaken by SACAT and other relevant bodies to ensure compliance with relevant acts for the protection and care of vulnerable persons subject to an order. - A risk register be established which records all acts or threats of self-harm by a child under the guardianship of the Chief Executive. There should be appropriate information sharing arrangements in place in relation to this risk register for all agencies that may deal with a child under the guardianship of the Minister including DCP, CAMHS, CPS, DECD and SAPOL. The risk register in relation to each child should be reviewed at regular intervals by an appropriately qualified professional with the ability to assess when a child may require closer assessment of suicidality and/or more intensive therapeutic treatment. Responses from the Department for Child Protection and the Department for Health and Wellbeing •   This recommendation requires further consideration. •   The Department for Child Protection is committed to therapeutic and trauma-informed practice. A range of safeguarding and risk management measures have been established since 2016, which offer services and supports for children and young people at risk, DCP will continue to explore opportunities for further improvement. •   A risk register of self-harm incidents reviewed in isolation of a deep understanding of a child or young person’s circumstances may not be the most effective way to achieve the intended outcomes. •   The State Government also has strong mechanisms for interagency collaboration focusing on the health and wellbeing of individual children and young people to ensure resources across the public sector are directed to areas of greatest need. 16 | P a g e OFFICIAL 2023-24 ANNUAL REPORT for the Coroners Court •   In recognition of the importance of ongoing risk management and safeguarding of children and young people in care, a review of the Department for Child Protection’s incident management system commenced in February 2019. A number of changes have since been implemented including the publication of new and updated guidance in relation to incidents in residential care, the establishment of the Significant Incident Reporting Unit, and the introduction of mandatory training related to significant incident reporting. •   In July 2023, the Department for Child Protection’s Manual of Practice was updated to incorporate additional

- CAMHS should review its policies and training regarding referrals, against the background of Zhane having not been referred, to ensure that cases requiring review are not missed. •   This recommendation is accepted. •   Progress has been made on the implementation of this recommendation. •   CAMHS has developed a standalone triage service named CONNECT. All children and young people under the care of Department for Child Protection (DCP) are referred to the CAMHS Specialist Guardianship team via CAMHS CONNECT. •   Referrals for early in-care children and young people are streamed to the collaborative Interagency Therapeutic Needs Panel (ITNP) meetings between CAMHS, DCP and the Department for Education (DFE). This provides an overarching review of the needs of the young people and ensures they are directed to the right service, in accordance with their needs. •   Young people who have been in DCP care for extended periods will be referred to CAMHS if required. Where appropriate, a referral to another, more clinically appropriate service, will be identified through the triage process.

- A review be undertaken of services available through CAMHS to children in state care, that the adequacy or otherwise of those services be assessed and that the necessary funding to enable provision of adequate services be determined.

- Implementation of recommendation 3 should include a scrutiny of the adequacy of funding for the Child and Adolescent Mental Health Service. •   Response to both 3 and 4. This recommendation is accepted. •   Various actions have been implemented or are in progress in response to these two recommendations. •   CAMHS has a dedicated Guardianship Service of 2.6 full time equivalent staff for children in state care, and all children/young people, including those in state care, can access CAMHS through their local community clinic or acute services. •   A strategic review of CAMHS is in progress, which includes services provided to children in state care. •   SA Health is working with all agencies to co-design a state-wide Child Protection Service Model of Care that incorporates the provision of therapeutic services for children and young people in care in relation to CAMHS service provision.

- There be a review of the payments made to family-based foster carers with a view to increasing the availability of family-based placements for children under guardianship of the Chief Executive. •   This recommendation is accepted in principle. •   Recognising the increasing costs of caring for children and young people, the 2023-24 State Budget included a 4.8% indexation for carer payments for all family based carers and a $50 fortnightly increase for general foster and kinship carers per child 16 and under, which represents an additional $32 million to foster and 17 | P a g e OFFICIAL 2023-24 ANNUAL REPORT for the Coroners Court kinship carers over the next four years. Further, an extra $4 million has been committed to increase the number of kinship care assessments undertaken. •   These additional financial commitments recognise the vital role carers play in supporting vulnerable children and young people. •   The Department for Child Protection is committed to growing family-based care and will continue to explore additional supports for carers, including exploring opportunities to improve the existing carer payment system. This work will also be guided by the recently established Carer Council, recommendations of Dr Fiona Arney’s December 2022 report on the Independent Inquiry into Foster and Kinship Care in South Australia and ongoing consultation with the carers.

- That the Department provide an initial psychological consultation for any child who is due to give evidence as an alleged victim, once the matter is listed for trial. The Department should inform the Witness Assistance Service at the ODPP who that psychologist is and ensure that the ODPP is properly informed about that child’s circumstances and any particular concerns there may be surrounding that child giving evidence as an alleged victim. •   These recommendations are accepted in principle. •   The Department for Child Protection is committed to ensuring that children and young people are provided with necessary supports prior to giving evidence in Court. The question of whether a child should receive therapeutic or specialist support at a particular point in time and the type of that support is entirely child-specific and is considered by the care team. •   If a child or young person does not already have a therapist, where a witness assistance officer has not been allocated or in circumstances where additional support may be required, the child or young person’s case worker will consult with the Department’s Psychological Services regarding the child or young person’s needs. •   The Department for Child Protection’s Manual of Practice will be updated to reflect this requirement and ensure that, in consultation with carers, children or young people who are due to give evidence as an alleged victim are appropriately supported. •   The Department for Child Protection consulted with the Office of the Director of Public Prosecutions (ODPP) in June 2023 to discuss and progress this recommendation.

- Each child under the guardianship of the Chief Executive must have their contact with biological family considered in detail in a meaningful way at least once every 12 months. This should include a consideration of contact with all siblings and biological parents. The relevant considerations should be documented in detail each year in the child’s Annual Review and saved on C3MS. •   This recommendation is accepted. •   The Children and Young People (Safety) Act 2017 (the CYPS Act), which was not in effect when Zhane was in care or at the time of his death, requires that all children and young people in care must have a case plan which includes a part setting out contact arrangements. The previous legislation – the Children’s Protection Act 1993 - which has been repealed, did not include a legislative requirement for case planning; this was undertaken as a matter of policy. •   Contact arrangements are reviewed as part of the child or young person’s regular case plan review. Case plans are reviewed and updated when circumstances change that impact the child or young person’s needs and/or where the case direction changes. At a minimum, case plans for children under long term guardianship must be reviewed at least six monthly. •   The CYPS Act requires the circumstances of a child or young person subject to a long- term guardianship order to be reviewed at least once a year. The annual review includes a review of the child or young person’s 18 | P a g e OFFICIAL 2023-24 ANNUAL REPORT for the Coroners Court contact arrangements. Recommendations made by the annual review panel are used to inform the actions and outcomes for the child or young person’s next case plan. The child or young person’s case plan and annual review are saved into the Department for Child Protection’s Connected Client and Case Management System (C3MS). •   The Department for Child Protection’s Manual of Practice contains additional guidance on supporting children and young people to develop and maintain family and community connections through contact arrangements and encourages workers to consider the role of contact arrangements in keeping Aboriginal children and young

.1 - A RATSIO (Recognised Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Organisation), as defined in, and gazetted pursuant to, subsection 12(8) of the Children and Young People (Safety) Act (2017) that is culturally connected to each Aboriginal child should be appointed for all such children at the point of intake into the child protection system.

.2 - The Department should implement a policy to ensure timely and proper consultation with a RATSIO, as required by subsection 12(3)(c) of the Children and Young People (Safety) Act (2017) where practicable, before all placement decisions are made.

.3 - In reporting the extent to which such children and young people have access to a case worker, community, relative or other person from the same Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander community as the child or young person, in compliance with Section 156 (1)(a)(iii) of the Children and Young People (Safety) Act (2017), the Department should specify the number of Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander children who have contact with a case worker, community, relative or other person from the same Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander community as the child or young person. •   These recommendations are accepted in principle. •   The South Australian Government recognises the importance of delivering on its commitments under the National Partnership Agreement on Closing the Gap and the Aboriginal Action Plan for the National Framework for Protecting Australia’s Children 2021-31 - Safe and Supported. •   The Department for Child Protection is also committed to acting in accordance with the Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Child Placement Principle (ATSICPP). •   It is noted that these recommendations (8.1-8.3) are specific to provisions contained in the Children and Young People (Safety) Act 2017 (CYPS Act). The Department’s current legislative reform work, which follows the recent review of that Act, is contemplating how to better embed the ATSICPP in legislation and practice, as well as to progress the national priorities of delegated decision-making to Aboriginal organisations, investment in Aboriginal-led service delivery and support of a culturally competent workforce. •   These efforts will be supported by the new South Australian Peak Body for Aboriginal Children and Young People, which will commence in mid-2024, and ongoing engagement with Aboriginal organisations, communities, families and children and young people. Further guidance will also be provided by Commissioner Lawrie’s ongoing Inquiry into the removal and placement of Aboriginal children and young people in care. •   The Department’s Manual of Practice also contains comprehensive guidance to reinforce the need for consultations with RATSIO’s to occur, where practicable, before placing an Aboriginal child or young person. The process for undertaking a consultation pursuant to section 12(3)(c) of the CYPS Act is outlined under its own key step in the Manual of Practice. 19 | P a g e

- That the current CALHN ACS Pathway be amended to a) include a step immediately after the Initial ECG requiring consideration of other serious causes of chest pain such as aortic dissection; and b) include the stipulation that a structured senior review should consider the possibility of other causes of chest pain and specifically refer to aortic dissection. Response from SA Health •   The recommendation has been accepted and the response incorporates actions by the relevant Local Health Networks (LHNs) and state-wide services, as detailed: •    Central Adelaide Local Health Network (CALHN) have amended their Acute Coronary Syndrome (ACS) Pathway in accordance with the Coroner’s recommendation. •    Metropolitan hospitals are reviewing their local procedures, pathways and protocols to ensure the consideration of other serious causes of chest pain, such as aortic dissection. These procedures include the plan for investigations and suspected diagnosis to be reviewed with the supervision of a senior clinician. •    The Women’s and Children’s Health Network (WCHN) are reviewing these recommendations in relation to women and children. Further discussion will be undertaken with the Cardiac, Obstetrics and Paediatric clinical areas. •    The Rural Support Service (RSS) plans to include these recommendations into the regional Acute Coronary Syndrome (ACS) Pathway. The pathway is managed by the Integrated Cardiovascular Clinical Network South Australia (iCCnetSA) team. The regional ACS Pathway currently incorporates a structured, senior cardiologist review, early in the pathway.

- That each Local Health Network in South Australia consider where appropriate developing a regular education program regarding aortic dissection presentations and its diagnosis, having regard to the recommendations in the paper by Professor Anne-Maree Kelly, ‘What Can Be Done to Improve Diagnosis of Aortic Dissection’. •   The recommendation has been accepted and this SA Health report incorporates the responses of the relevant LHNs and statewide services, as detailed: •    All SA Health LHNs provide education sessions to their clinical staff about coronary artery disease, heart failure and acute coronary syndrome. •    Education is delivered in the following ways: •     Registered Medical Officer (RMO) rotational teaching program and General Practitioner (GP) consultant program •     On-line presentations and recordings •     Grand Round presentations •     Articles, newsletters, and on-line resources •     Structured emergency education sessions •    Those sites that do not currently include the diagnosis and management of aortic dissection are in the process of developing training resources to address this specifically. •    Professor Ann-Maree Kelly’s paper on improving the diagnosis of aortic dissection has been provided to all SA Health LHNs to consider the recommendations in review of their education programs. 20 | P a g e OFFICIAL 2023-24 ANNUAL REPORT for the Coroners Court Latouche Mazzei, Lucas (Coroner White)

- The Department for Education is directed to review its policy and procedures for obtaining and sharing information concerning students with special needs and/or medical conditions to enable teaching staff of that student to become aware, at the earliest opportunity, about how the student needs to be cared for during his or her attendance at a school day or school sanctioned event. This review should also undertake to examine and implement a procedure for easy and quick access of that information by the student’s teaching staff. In conducting this review it is recommended that the Minister for Education, Training and Skills consider the evidence presented at this Inquest from Catholic Education South Australia and St Patricks Special School, Dulwich. Responses from the Department for Education •   The recommendation has been accepted. •   The Department for Education has undertaken the requested review and have developed a Practice Guide on supporting children with a disability as they transition to a new preschool or school. The document articulates evidence-based strategies and advice to improve the preparedness of the site to support children and students with a disability, including the transfer of information regarding student needs and relevant medical records. •   The adoption of the practice guide is being supported through the roll out of a new school and preschool administrative system, the Education Management System, which will automate the transfer of student information from one government preschool or school to another when the enrolment of the student in the new site is confirmed. 314 preschools and 142 schools have been migrated from their respective legacy administration systems as at December 1, 2023. The project team is working to have the new system implemented in all government schools and preschools by the end of 2025.

- All teaching staff be required to hold up-to-date qualifications in providing first aid assistance in an education and care setting. •   The recommendation is accepted in principle. •   The department has explored several policy settings in developing the response to the Deputy Coroner’s recommendation. •   As part of this review, the department considered: •    the Deputy Coroner’s intentions regarding the scope of ‘all teaching staff’ to determine if it related to ‘teachers’ or included other employee cohorts for the department such as SSOs •    the Deputy Coroner’s intentions regarding the scope of ‘up-to-date qualifications in providing first aid assistance in an education and care setting’ given the range of first aid certificates available •    the different risk profiles that exist across different education settings. •   In responding to this recommendation, the department will adopt a phased approached commencing with the provision of the appropriate first aid training to all staff (not just teachers as recommended by the Deputy Coroner) who work in special education settings and increasing the provision of first aid training in other settings to achieve a ratio of 1 qualified first aider for every 50 adults and students on site. This will include the requirement those first aiders to hold current qualifications, including annual CPR refreshers. •   It is anticipated that moving towards a 1:50 ratio inclusive of staff, students and volunteers will require an additional 2,740 trained first aiders in government schools and preschools. Based on the volume of training required, we expect this first phase of the response to be completed in 2025. •   Once completed, we will undertake a further review of our first aid training policy to inform next steps. •   This change strengthens the controls in special education settings comparable with the training delivered at St Patrick’s Special School. It also strengthens the department’s current policy settings and requires CPR refresher training annually. 21 | P a g e OFFICIAL 2023-24 ANNUAL REPORT for the Coroners Court

- The first aid guidelines for a choking emergency are reviewed and amended to reflect those of the Australian Resuscitation Council, in particular concerning a first responders actions if the person choking becomes unresponsive. •   The recommendation has been accepted. •   The Oral Eating and Drinking Procedure provides direction for all staff working in education and care to plan and manage children and young people who require oral eating and drinking support including oral sensitivities or fixation, pica, swallowing disorders, feeding, food phobia and choking. •   The department has reviewed the procedure’s and specifically updated the sections on food and drink storage and choking risk minimisation strategies. The first aid advice within the procedure reflects that of the Australian Resuscitation Council.

- All telecommunication equipment for teaching staff be portable to allow the device to be taken by the first aid responder to the person in distress. •   The recommendation has been accepted in principle. •   As of June 2023, there were approximately 2,900 mobile telecommunication devices provided to government schools. The department is further investigating mobile phone coverage across all sites to identify where coverage blackspots may exist and will look to install a cordless telephone in these locations. •   The department will be updating the design standards that inform the design of new schools and preschools and the construction of new facilities at existing government schools and preschools in 2024. This will include the inclusion of a portable telephone in disability units. •   The Practice Guide, referenced in the response to recommendation 1 above, also prompts schools and preschools with existing disability units or special options settings to consider mobile communications equipment as part of the planning process for students with disability or complex health conditions.

- The Department’s policy and procedures are reviewed and amended for the safe storing and consumption of food and drinks within its educational sites and for events sanctioned by the Department. •   The recommendation has been accepted. •   The Oral Eating and Drinking Procedure (as mentioned under Recommendation 2) has been updated to specifically provide guidance and direction on the safe storage of food and drink for students who are within the scope of the procedure. The department liaised with the Women’s and Children’s Health Network in making these updates. Comment from the Department for Education •   In response to the Deputy Coroner’s findings, the department has also undertaken the following actions (which were not specifically recommended by the Deputy Coroner): •    A new “Managing critical incidents of an extreme nature policy” and related procedure have been developed. These documents set out that when a critical incident occurs at a site, a group of appropriate departmental leaders will meet to provide an immediate response and reporting of an incident. A new “Incident Support Leader” role has been created; this role will act as a point of contact in relation to the incident, investigate the incident with site leadership, evaluate and identify areas for improvement to prevent like incidents recurring, and liaise with relevant staff to communicate findings and initiate appropriate changes to policy or practice. An experienced former education director has been appointed to this role. •    A new procedure has been developed “Supporting bereaved parents and caregivers”. The procedure sets out that department engagement with families should be guided by the Australian Open Disclosure Framework, and that shared information should be accurate, factual, relevant and devoid of speculation. 22 | P a g e OFFICIAL 2023-24 ANNUAL REPORT for the Coroners Court •     The department has reviewed the duty of care guideline to place greater emphasis on the importance of supervision and the matters and educator should turn their mind to when considering what adequate

- The Minister urges the Australian Committee of the International Academies of Emergency Dispatch to give urgent consideration to updating the Australasian procedures of the Pro Q/A software with respect to instructions being provided to a responder of a child or adult choking and conscious to be consistent with the Australian Resuscitation Council Guidelines. •    The recommendation has been accepted. •    South Australia Ambulance Service (SAAS) is collaborating with the International Academies of Emergency Dispatch to review the event with a view to updating the Australasian procedures and instructions to be consistent with the Australian Resuscitation Council (ARC) Guidelines.

- The Minister directs the SA Ambulance Service to review its training and procedures to be consistent with the Australian Resuscitation Council Guidelines, in particular to review whether the Heimlich manoeuvre, as described, should be recommended to a first responder which is contrary to the Australian Resuscitation Council recommendations. •    The recommendation has been accepted. •    Following completion of recommendation 1, SAAS will review their local training and procedures to align with the International Academies of Emergency Dispatch procedures and instructions. This work will give particular consideration to the incorporation or not, of the Heimlich manoeuvre, as part of the first responder’s procedure. Leong Yi Hui, Adelene (Coroner White)

- It is recommended that the Minister receive formal advice from the AIHS and SafeWork: 1)   Concerning the urgent need for reform of the regulation and governance of amusement rides and devices in Australia; 2)   To urge the creation and implementation in all Australian jurisdictions of: i)    A nationwide regulatory process to verify and record design registrations for amusement devices and rides to ensure that every amusement device and ride in Australia is subject to the same process of design registration; ii)   A common application procedure for plant registration to ensure that every plant registration has met the same criteria, regardless of where it is registered in Australia; iii) A law or regulation that plant registration will not be granted unless a design registration certificate has been endorsed and verified by the State or Territory regulator; iv) A national database of design registration numbers and plant registration numbers that is accessible by regulators of all States and Territories; v)    A nationwide panel of qualified persons be established to assess, annually, the skills of competent persons inspecting amusement rides and devices to verify which aspects of expertise the competent person possesses; 23 | P a g e OFFICIAL 2023-24 ANNUAL REPORT for the Coroners Court vi) An annual assessment of the competent persons including a requirement of mandatory participation in a continuing education scheme; vii) A mandatory national electronic logbook system for all amusement devices and rides in Australia that can be accessed by all authorised people necessary for inspections and audits in any jurisdiction; viii) Laws to ensure the logbook for an amusement ride or device must include a design registration certificate, a plant registration certificate and a statement from the manufacturer of the device or ride confirming their criteria for eligibility of patrons to use the ride or device;

- The appointment of an independent Board of Inquiry by the Executive Government to undertake a comprehensive review of the key findings and to make recommendations to government with particular emphasis on: a)   The content and delivery of restraint training to correctional officers at Yatala. b)   The content and delivery of training for supervisory roles. c)   Performance review processes (or the lack thereof). d)   The enforcement of refresher training in restraint, first aid and cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR). e)   Risk management processes. f)   Record keeping requirements (electronic and hard copy) with particular emphasis on records relating to risk assessment, and the feasibility of moving from paper-based records to electronic records. 25 | P a g e OFFICIAL 2023-24 ANNUAL REPORT for the Coroners Court Responses from the Department For Correctional Services and South Australia Police •   In addition to intensive internal investigations, this incident has been subject to external and independent scrutiny including a full investigation initiated by the Ombudsman of South Australia, as well as the Coronial process. •   The Ombudsman’s investigation resulted in 17 detailed recommendations, all of which were considered by the DCS Investigations Review Committee and aligned with the Department’s Action Plan. All 17 recommendations have been implemented. •   In consideration of the passage of time following Mr Morrison’s death, and in the context of all the critical review work already undertaken by the Department, including the implementation of a range of security and process improvements, a further independent review is not supported by the agency. •   The Minister with responsibility for Correctional Services will however engage Mr Peter Severin, as an independent correctional expert, to conduct a desktop review of the Department’s response with respect to the specific recommendations made by the Deputy State Coroner.

- Correctional Officers be prohibited from undertaking operational duties which require contact with prisoners UNLESS AND UNTIL they have completed the DCS Control Restraint Defensive Training program AND: a)     The correctional officer has completed DCS refresher training on or before the date it falls due. b)     The correctional officer holds a current First Aid certificate. c)     The correctional officer has completed an annual renewal of the CPR component of first aid training and holds a valid CPR qualification on or before the date it falls due. •   From the time of this incident, a comprehensive review and enhancement of Correctional Officer (CO) mandatory training has been undertaken. DCS has since implemented advanced systems to monitor mandatory training validity, alongside more robust rostering. •   In 2020, the Department introduced the Learning Academy, which has the responsibility for strategic workforce planning and delivery of a range of learning and development opportunities across the agency. •   Within the Learning Academy sits a Mandatory Training Team who has oversight of the compulsory training via a Mandatory Training Matrix, which identifies and aligns to the employees’ position within the Department. This includes Control Restraint Defensive Training (CRDT) which is mandatory every three years to ensure currency of restraint and defensive techniques are maintained. •   DCS will impose limitations on the duties that can be undertaken by a CO in the event relevant training has not been completed, for example, certain posts will be excluded for a CO if mandatory training requirements have not been met. Staff will also be ineligible for opportunities unless mandated training requirements are met. •   The Department strives to provide and manage a safe and secure custodial environment and it is therefore necessary to have appropriate levels of staffing for an immediate response in the event of a critical incident. Subsequently, staff who have not met their mandatory training requirements will not be precluded from other face-to-face operational roles. 26 | P a g e OFFICIAL

- That an expiry date for restraint, first aid and CPR training be recorded on the rear of correctional officers’ identity tags in tamper proof form. •   DCS considers that a hardcopy-based, static approach is not practical, and poses risk. •   DCS has implemented a robust digital training recording system and invested in a new state-of-the-art rostering system that will also enhance the agency’s visibility of a CO’s training status. •   The new rostering system is expected to be implemented in mid-2024.

- That resuscitation equipment including automatic external defibrillators (‘AEDs’) be placed in all areas of Yatala Labour Prison which manage the arrival of prisoners (e.g. the G Division sally port). •   AEDs are now installed in all areas of Yatala Labour Prison which manage the arrival of prisoners. In addition, the Adelaide Remand Centre, as the primary admission prison for the correctional system in South Australia, has AEDs installed in all prisoner arrival areas. •   DCS will also meet the requirements prescribed by the External Defibrillators (Public Access) Act 2022 (AED Act) for an AED to be installed for every 1200m2 of floor area. A correctional institution is a designated building or facility under this legislation.

- The repeal of legislative provisions of the Correctional Services Act 1982 which enable the Holden Hill police cells and/or other similar facilities to be declared as ‘a prison’ or ‘a police prison’ or proclaimed for such use. •   Section 18 of the Correctional Services Act 1982 (the Act) provides that the Governor may declare premises to be prisons or police prisons. Various police stations have been declared to be police prisons for the purpose of section 18 of the Act through the Correctional Services Act (Declaration of Police Prisons) Proclamation 2007 (the Proclamation). •   The Department has not utilised police cells since 23 May 2018 and the Holden Hill Police Cells have been decommissioned by the South Australia Police (SAPOL). •   An important safeguard as part of the Department’s custodial surge demand management strategy, is the ability to utilise SAPOL police cells during periods of high demand on prisoner numbers. •   In place of repealing the legislative powers of section 18 of the Act, the Department will seek to issue a new Proclamation for the purposes of section 18 of the Act that will only reference current police cells.

- Recommendations 2-10 inclusive made by Deputy Coroner White in the inquest into the death of Joshua Marek STACHOR be implemented in full. •   The Department confirms recommendations 2-10 in relation to Mr Stachor have been accepted and progress of these recommendations is being monitored through the Investigations Review Committee. All required actions are being completed through enhancements of the Standard Operating Procedures and processes relevant to managing prisoners at risk of suicide and self-harm.

- Subject to security and health considerations, I recommend that all first-time Aboriginal prisoners must be placed in a shared cell. I recommend that if for any reason such prisoners are to be relocated to a single cell the SA Prison Health Service should be immediately notified. •   The Department is supportive of this recommendation in the context of newly admitted prisoners, and changes will be made to the DCS case management and admissions processes to provide that first-time Aboriginal prisoners will, where possible, be placed in a shared cell. 27 | P a g e OFFICIAL 2023-24 ANNUAL REPORT for the Coroners Court •   This however is only if the shared placement is considered safe following a prisoner’s admissions risk and health assessment, undertaken in conjunction with the South Australian Prison Health Services (SAPHS) and will require ongoing, close liaison with SAPHS.

- Information pamphlets and/or other printed material be provided to all Aboriginal prisoners on admission or in their accommodation units setting out in detail the availability and operation of Aboriginal health and liaison services within the correctional facility. •   Improvements have been made to ensure Aboriginal prisoners are identified as early as possible in the admission process and access to Aboriginal Liaison Officers (ALOs) is provided. An information pamphlet outlining the services of ALOs was circulated to all prison sites on 28 August 2023. The pamphlet is displayed in common areas, family visits centres and near prisoner kiosks.

- Noting that SAPOL officers who are stationed at Holden Hill are usually the first responders to any incidents at Yatala Labour Prison, I recommend that all officers who are inducted into the Holden Hill Local Service Area attend at Yatala for the purpose of their details being entered onto the biometric data base to facilitate entry to the prison during such incidents. •   The Department confirms the biometrics registration system is available to SAPOL officers. On 31 October 2023, 1,329 SAPOL officers had been registered on the DCS biometrics system and SAPOL is developing a Statewide policy of registrations at prisons to support this recommendation ongoing. SAPOL has advised however that due to the logistics of having officers move through operations rapidly, at times, it may be difficult to capture a 100% coverage. In June 2023, following a meeting between DCS and South Australia Police, the process commenced for all permanent Holden Hill police to record their biometrics with DCS. The requirement for biometrics recording for new members is now included within SAPOL’s Holden Hill Induction policy. SAPOL notes in the event of an immediate police response event, police will not be required to undergo biometric scanning. This was recently experienced in July 2023 when officers from Major Crime Investigation Section (amongst others) entered YLP in response to a murder. Corrections officers recorded the identity of police in and out of the prison negating the need for biometric scanning.

- I recommend that the DCS enter into discussions with the Public Service Association and the Correctional Officers Legal Fund with a view to developing a Memorandum of Understanding directed at the implementation of procedures which ensure prompt access to legal advice by correctional officers (and other Department employees) in the event of future incidents at Yatala Labour Prison. •   The safety of staff and prisoners is paramount to the Department and the focus in the event of a critical incident is to provide a prompt response that ensures the security and good order of the institution. DCS considers this recommendation to be inconsistent with that area of focus and therefore does not support this recommendation. Paxford, Matthew George (Coroner Whittle)

- To the Minister for Health and Wellbeing I recommend that ensuite bathroom doors in acute inpatient mental health units be reviewed to identify potential ligature points and be removed, modified or replaced to eliminate potential ligature points. Response from SA Health •   The recommendation has been accepted and this SA Health report incorporates the responses of the Office of the Chief Psychiatrist (OCP), in consultation with the Local Health Networks (LHNs) and relevant statewide services, as detailed: •    The ensuite doors at the Mount Gambier IMHIU have been removed and a trial of quick release saloons doors is currently being undertaken. 28 | P a g e OFFICIAL 2023-24 ANNUAL REPORT for the Coroners Court •    A Safety Notice was distributed to all LHNs on 31 March 2023 with a request for each LHN to complete an audit of doors and other relevant ligature points. A response has been received from all LHNs with mental health inpatient units where ensuite doors have been in situ and have been removed. •    Further discussion on this issue is planned for the July 2023 Strategic Mental Health Quality Improvement Committee.
